# Diagnosing a No-Start Condition on a 2008 Chevrolet Cobalt: Beyond the Starter Relay

When a vehicle exhibits symptoms where accessories power up, lights function, but cranking engagement fails despite a confirmed functional starter motor, the diagnostic path quickly narrows from mechanical failure to electrical architecture issues. In the specific case of a 2008 Chevrolet Cobalt with less than 110 kilometers on the odometer, which has been stationary with the battery disconnected for over a month, we are dealing with a classic "no crank, no start" scenario that often points to the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) or its fuel delivery interface.

The user observed that switching the starter relay had no effect, yet jumping the relay connections successfully engaged the starter motor. This is a critical data point: the starter solenoid and mechanical engagement are healthy. The issue lies upstream in the signal path required to trigger that engagement or downstream in the engine's ability to sustain combustion once spinning.

### The PCM Fuel Pump Control Circuit

A primary suspect in this configuration is the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) itself, specifically its internal fuel pump control circuit. On General Motors vehicles of this era, the PCM often controls the fuel pump relay directly via an internal transistor switch rather than relying solely on an external relay triggered by a simple ignition signal. If the PCM's internal driver for the fuel pump relay has failed, the engine may crank (if the starter is jumped) but will not prime the fuel system.

The symptom of the car running for a day or so after starting usually indicates that the vehicle retained enough residual pressure in the fuel rail to fire on initial cranks, only to stall once the PCM failed to re-engage the fuel pump during operation. The fact that disconnecting and reconnecting the battery temporarily resolved the issue suggests a latch-up condition within the PCM's power supply or a protective shutdown triggered by voltage anomalies when the battery was disconnected.

### Ignition Switch and Security System Verification

The observation that accessories remain on after removing the key, with only battery disconnection able to reset the system, strongly points to an ignition switch failure or a corrupted security state. In many GM platforms of this generation, the ignition switch contains multiple contacts for different positions (ACC, ON, RUN). If the "RUN" contact is worn or corroded, the PCM may not receive the ground reference required to enable fuel injection and ignition timing, even if 12V power is present for the stereo.

However, before condemning the PCM, one must rule out the Passlock system. The Cobalt uses a passive anti-theft feature that disables the fuel pump unless it detects a valid key signature via the Hall effect sensor in the ignition lock cylinder. If the sensor is misaligned or the ring gear teeth are damaged, the PCM will inhibit fuel delivery indefinitely until reset. A simple disconnect of the battery does not always clear a persistent Passlock fault code stored in non-volatile memory if the trigger condition persists.

### Diagnostic Strategy and Trade-offs

The recommendation to replace the "electronic portion of the ignition" for $47 aligns with replacing the entire ignition switch assembly, which often includes the key cylinder and sensor ring. This is a cost-effective intervention compared to PCM replacement or reprogramming. However, if the ignition switch is replaced and the issue persists, the focus must shift to the PCM.

If the fuel pump relay control pin on the PCM is confirmed dead (no voltage output when cranking) and the external relay test was inconclusive due to a bad internal driver, the PCM is likely the culprit. The trade-off here is significant: replacing the PCM involves cloning the VIN, ECU code, and immobilizer keys, which requires specialized equipment and time.

### Final Verification Steps

Before committing to expensive repairs, verify the fuel pump operation by listening for the distinct hum from the rear of the vehicle within 2â3 seconds of turning the key to the ON position (before cranking). If there is no sound, and the ignition switch has been ruled out, the PCM's internal fuel pump driver circuit is almost certainly failed. In this specific Cobalt, the intermittent nature of the problem suggests thermal expansion or moisture ingress affecting a solder joint or internal component within the PCM, which explains why it worked for short periods after a battery disconnect reset.

Addressing these electrical architecture issues requires methodical isolation of the control signals from the power delivery components. The starter relay jump confirmed the mechanical side is sound; now the focus is entirely on the electronic command path and the security logic governing fuel delivery.
